stories.title: Choosing the intensity and the duration of endocrine treatment
stories.premise: Almost everyone in this cell is cured by local treatment and endocrine therapy, and the recurrences arrive over two decades rather than two years. So the adjuvant questions are not whether to treat but how hard, for how long, and for whom the extra years or the extra drug are worth their cost.

chapters.title: Adjuvant endocrine therapy in hormone receptor-positive disease

questions.ask: How completely does oestrogen have to be removed?
questions.rationale: Tamoxifen blocks the receptor; an aromatase inhibitor removes the ligand; ovarian suppression removes the source. Each step is a deeper intervention on the same axis, and each was expected to buy more disease control at more cost.
questions.experiment: Direct comparisons of an aromatase inhibitor against tamoxifen, and of ovarian suppression added to either, in premenopausal and postmenopausal populations separately.
questions.finding: Deeper suppression lowers recurrence, and the absolute gain tracks baseline risk rather than being uniform across the cell.
questions.limitation: None of these trials randomised the decision that a clinic actually makes, which is whether this particular patient's risk justifies the menopausal symptoms and the bone loss. Subgroup gradients are not the same as a randomised selection rule.
questions.next: If the benefit tracks risk, can risk be measured well enough to allocate the intensity rather than infer it after the fact?

questions.ask: How long should endocrine treatment continue?
questions.rationale: Recurrence in this cell continues at a roughly constant rate for at least twenty years, so treatment that stops at five years stops while the hazard is still running.
questions.experiment: Randomised extension beyond five years — tamoxifen to ten, an aromatase inhibitor after tamoxifen, an aromatase inhibitor after an aromatase inhibitor — and, against the same question from the other side, trials of shorter or intermittent extension.
questions.finding: Extension lowers recurrence, the effect is smaller than the first five years bought, and several extension trials found that more was not better than less.
questions.limitation: The extension trials enrolled patients who had already tolerated five years, which is a selected population, and they differ in the drug taken first, so the results are not interchangeable across sequences.
questions.next: Since the benefit of extension is real but small, can the patients who get it be identified before ten years of treatment are prescribed to everyone?

questions.ask: Does adding a CDK4/6 inhibitor to adjuvant endocrine therapy lower recurrence?
questions.rationale: CDK4/6 inhibition roughly doubles progression-free survival in metastatic hormone receptor-positive disease, and the cells that seed a late recurrence are the same lineage. If the drug works on macroscopic disease it should work on residual disease.
questions.experiment: Four trials added a CDK4/6 inhibitor to adjuvant endocrine therapy, differing in the drug, the duration, and how high the enrolled risk was.
questions.finding: Two showed a durable improvement in invasive disease-free survival and two did not, and the split follows the specific drug, schedule and risk population rather than the class.
questions.limitation: These are not head-to-head trials. The populations, the treatment durations and the endpoints differ enough that the divergence cannot be attributed to the molecule alone, and overall survival is immature.
questions.next: If escalation only pays at high risk, what is the risk threshold, and does it have to be measured before treatment or can it be read from the response to treatment?

questions.ask: Can the decision to give chemotherapy be made on biology rather than on anatomy?
questions.rationale: Node count and tumour size measure how long a cancer has been growing, not how much it depends on oestrogen. A genomic assay measures the second, which is what predicts whether cytotoxic treatment adds anything to endocrine treatment.
questions.experiment: Randomised trials that assigned chemotherapy by a genomic score rather than by stage, in node-negative and then node-positive disease, with survival as the endpoint.
questions.finding: A large fraction of this cell can omit chemotherapy without losing disease control, and the exceptions cluster by age and menopausal status rather than by score alone.
questions.limitation: The assays were validated on populations treated with the endocrine therapy of their era, and the age effect is confounded with ovarian function, so the benefit attributed to chemotherapy may partly be the benefit of chemotherapy-induced menopause.
questions.next: If a score taken once before treatment can allocate chemotherapy, can the tumour's own response to a short course of endocrine therapy allocate it better?

questions.ask: Can the response to treatment be used to allocate treatment, rather than the baseline alone?
questions.rationale: A baseline assay predicts; a short course of endocrine therapy tests. A tumour whose proliferation collapses under two weeks of an aromatase inhibitor has demonstrated the dependence the assay was trying to infer.
questions.experiment: Response-adapted designs that give a brief endocrine exposure, measure the change in proliferation, and route patients to chemotherapy or to endocrine treatment on what they see.
questions.finding: Response separates the population, and the endocrine-responsive group does well on endocrine treatment alone.
questions.limitation: A dynamic marker predicts outcome in a cohort that has already been selected on it, so the comparison is against a historical expectation rather than against the same patients treated the other way.
questions.next: Does adding CDK4/6 inhibition to the induction course change who looks responsive, and is that change real or an artefact of a drug that suppresses proliferation in everyone?
